fields.Front: Define cohesion and coupling in one sentence each, and say which is 'inside' and which is 'between'.
fields.Back: Cohesion: how closely related the functions and responsibilities within a single module are, i.e. the degree to which elements inside a module belong together. Coupling: the degree of dependency between modules, i.e. how closely two classes or components are connected. Cohesion is within; coupling is between.

fields.Front: What characterises high cohesion, and which SOLID principle does it follow?
fields.Back: Responsibilities are closely related and focused on a single task, following the Single Responsibility Principle. The payoff is that when something must change, the change is isolated to one module.

fields.Front: Give the slides' example of a highly cohesive class and say what would ruin it.
fields.Back: ShoppingCart is cohesive if all its methods (addItem(), removeItem(), calculateTotal()) are directly related to managing the cart. Adding sendMarketingEmail(), generateInvoicePDF(), or logUserActivity() would spread it across unrelated tasks and destroy the cohesion.

fields.Front: What goes wrong with low cohesion?
fields.Back: Responsibilities are spread across multiple unrelated tasks, which makes modules harder to maintain because changing one part of the module can inadvertently affect other, unrelated parts.

fields.Front: What does low coupling mean, and which SOLID principle does it follow?
fields.Back: Modules are mostly independent, so changes in one module have minimal impact on others. It follows the Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level modules should depend on abstractions rather than on concrete implementations.

fields.Front: Describe the two mixed cohesion/coupling combinations.
fields.Back: High cohesion + high coupling: modules are internally well-organized but have strong dependencies on other modules, so changes still ripple between them. Low cohesion + low coupling: modules are independent but poorly organized internally, each a grab-bag of unrelated tasks.

fields.Front: Which combination describes 'modules are independent, but each is a grab-bag of unrelated tasks'?
Why do cohesion and coupling matter for the rest of the course?
fields.Back: They are the measures of design quality that justify almost every later topic: SOLID principles, design patterns, and testability can all be argued for as 'this increases cohesion' or 'this reduces coupling'. They apply to any module: a class, component, file, or service.

fields.Text: High cohesion is important for ease of {{c1::understanding}}, ease of {{c1::maintenance}}, and {{c1::reusability}}.
fields.Extra: A class that does one thing can be read in one sentence, its changes are localized, and it can be dropped into another context without dragging unrelated baggage along.

fields.Text: Low coupling is important for ease of {{c1::maintenance}}, {{c1::flexibility}}, and {{c1::testing}}.
fields.Extra: Change one module without a ripple of edits; swap one implementation for another (PayPal for Stripe); test a class in isolation by substituting fake collaborators.

fields.Text: The ideal design is {{c1::high}} cohesion plus {{c1::low}} coupling; the worst case is {{c1::low}} cohesion plus {{c1::high}} coupling.
{{c1::Cohesion}} measures how well elements inside one module belong together; {{c1::coupling}} measures the degree of dependency between modules. The goal is {{c1::high cohesion, low coupling}}.
fields.Extra: Students frequently swap the two on exams.

fields.Text: High cohesion follows the {{c1::Single Responsibility Principle}}; low coupling follows the {{c1::Dependency Inversion Principle}}; extensibility follows the {{c1::Open/Closed Principle}}.
A cohesive ShoppingCart has methods {{c1::addItem(), removeItem(), calculateTotal()}} - all focused solely on cart-related activities.
